books.section: Topic 4.3 Politics and Regional Interests, C. A Temporary Truce on the Slavery Question in the Pre-Civil War Period

stimulus.text:
Thomas Jefferson, retired at Monticello, wrote to Congressman John Holmes about the Missouri question on April 22, 1820:

“but this momentous question, like a fire bell in the night, awakened and filled me with terror. I considered it at once as the knell of the Union. it is hushed indeed for the moment. but this is a reprieve only, not a final sentence. a geographical line, coinciding with a marked principle, moral and political, once conceived and held up to the angry passions of men, will never be obliterated; and every new irritation will mark it deeper and deeper.”
stimulus.source_note: Thomas Jefferson to John Holmes, April 22, 1820; text verified against Founders Online and the Library of Congress. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from Jefferson to John Holmes, April 22, 1820 (public domain, verified against Founders Online)
stem: Jefferson compares the Missouri question to “a fire bell in the night” mainly to show that

options.text: Missouri’s application for statehood had caught Congress by surprise in 1818
options.misconception: The fight had been building since Missouri applied in 1818; nothing here says Congress was surprised.

options.text: the Compromise had settled the slavery question for good
options.misconception: Jefferson says the quiet is “a reprieve only, not a final sentence”; settled is the opposite of his point.

options.text: a line over slavery would keep dividing Americans after the debate ended
the Union would break apart before the year was over
options.misconception: Jefferson warns of danger ahead, not a dated prediction; “knell of the Union” is his fear, not a timetable.

rationales.A: The Missouri fight had been running since 1818, when Missouri applied for statehood. Surprise is not Jefferson’s point; the alarm is.
rationales.B: Jefferson says the question “is hushed indeed for the moment” but calls that “a reprieve only, not a final sentence.” A settled question needs no reprieve.
rationales.C: The fire bell is an alarm, and the line is what keeps ringing: Jefferson says the geographical line “will never be obliterated” and that every new irritation will mark it deeper. The line itself, not just the moment, is the danger.
rationales.D: Jefferson calls the question the “knell of the Union,” which is a warning about the future, not a date. He writes as a man afraid of what comes next, not as a prophet of 1820.
rationales.general:
1. Find the image. A fire bell in the night is an alarm that wakes a sleeping town.
2. Note the time words. The question is “hushed indeed for the moment,” but that is “a reprieve only, not a final sentence.”
3. Note what lasts. Jefferson says the geographical line “will never be obliterated” and every new irritation will mark it deeper.
4. Put it together. The alarm is about the line, which keeps the fight alive after the debate ends.
Background: Missouri applied for statehood as a slave state in 1818, when free and slave states stood eleven to eleven.
Remember: when a writer uses an alarm image, ask what keeps ringing after the noise stops.
